title: Case design techniques: equivalence partitioning and boundary values

videos.script: Six tickets. The theatre's rule says one to six per order. {{rule}} How many different things could somebody type into that field? Every whole number, every word, and nothing at all. {{infinite}} You cannot try them all, and you do not need to. Most values behave exactly like their neighbours. {{classes}} Equivalence partitioning groups the values the rule treats alike, and tests one from each group. {{partitions}} Boundary value analysis then goes to the edges between the groups. {{edges}} That is where a programmer writes less than, and meant less than or equal. {{off-by-one}} Each case you write then says which group it came from, so somebody else can see why it exists. {{why}} In this lesson you apply both techniques to a new account's name and password, and to the number of tickets in an order. {{apply}} Two of the values you choose break boxoffice. {{two}} One sits exactly on a boundary. The other is not a number at all. {{defects}}
